nameStory: This lichen gets its "blistered" name from the puffy, bubble-like bumps that cover its surface, making it look like it's been burned or had blisters form on its skin. The "rock tripe" part comes from its leathery, stomach-lining-like texture that reminded early naturalists of the edible tripe used in cooking. Indigenous peoples and Arctic explorers actually did eat rock tripes during times of scarcity, though they're quite tough and bitter!
description: Blistered Rock Tripe is a fascinating lichen that looks like a piece of dark, leathery skin stuck to rocks. This unusual organism is actually two life forms living together - a fungus and algae working as partners to survive in harsh conditions. The lichen forms circular to irregularly shaped patches that can grow several inches across, with a distinctive bumpy, blistered surface that feels rough and papery when dry. It's typically dark brown to blackish on top, creating dramatic contrast against pale rock surfaces.

idTips.label: Blistered Surface
idTips.description: The top surface is covered with distinctive puffy bumps and blisters that feel rough and papery when touched - like touching bubble wrap that's been painted dark brown

idTips.label: Single Attachment Point
idTips.description: The entire lichen attaches to rock at just one central point underneath, like an umbrella stem - you can often lift the edges and feel this connection

idTips.label: Dark Coloration
idTips.description: Upper surface ranges from dark brown to nearly black, sometimes with grayish patches, creating stark contrast against light-colored rocks

idTips.label: Leathery Texture
idTips.description: When dry, feels brittle and papery with a slight crackling sound when handled; becomes more pliable and rubbery when wet from rain or snow

idTips.label: Rock Habitat
idTips.description: Always grows directly on exposed rock surfaces, never on soil, wood, or other surfaces - particularly favors granite and other acidic rocks in exposed locations

habitat: Look for Blistered Rock Tripe on exposed rock faces and cliff surfaces in New England's mountains, particularly in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and higher elevations of Vermont and western Massachusetts. It thrives on acidic rocks like granite in areas that experience harsh weather conditions - windy ridges, rocky summits, and north-facing cliff faces where few other organisms can survive. These hardy lichens are indicators of clean air and pristine mountain environments.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more noticeable as snow melts away from rock faces, revealing the dark patches that contrast sharply with wet, light-colored granite. The lichen may appear slightly more pliable from spring moisture.
seasonality.summer: Most visible during dry periods when the dark, blistered surface creates maximum contrast against sun-bleached rocks. Touch reveals the characteristic papery, brittle texture at its most pronounced.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible and identifiable, often appearing darker against the changing landscape. The blistered texture becomes very apparent as autumn's lower humidity keeps the lichen dry and crispy.
seasonality.winter: Still present and identifiable on exposed rock faces above treeline, though may be partially obscured by snow and ice. When visible, the dark patches stand out dramatically against white snow.

funFact: This tough lichen can literally freeze solid and still survive - scientists have found that rock tripes can withstand temperatures down to -40°F and then spring back to life when conditions improve, making them some of the most cold-hardy organisms on Earth!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Smooth Rock Tripe, but the blistered species has those distinctive puffy bumps while Smooth Rock Tripe has a relatively flat, unblistered surface. Memory trick: if it looks like it has chicken pox or bubble wrap texture, it's the blistered variety!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they're plants, lichens are neither plants nor animals - they're a remarkable partnership between fungi and algae living as one organism. This cooperation allows them to colonize harsh environments where neither partner could survive alone, making rock tripes some of nature's ultimate survivors.
compareHints: Blistered Rock Tripe stands out from other rock tripes by its distinctly bumpy, pustule-covered surface - most other species in the genus have smoother tops. While Smooth Rock Tripe lives in similar rocky habitats, it lacks the characteristic blisters, and Frosted Rock Tripe has a more grayish, powdery appearance rather than the dark, bubble-textured surface of the blistered species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's rock tripes, smooth rock tripe lives up to its name with the least textured upper surface.
Lesser Rocktripe is smaller and has a more uniformly wrinkled surface compared to Greater Salted Rocktripe, which can grow much larger and often has distinctive holes or perforations.

Among New England's rock tripes, peppered rock tripe is distinguished by its granular black dots on the surface - smooth rock tripe lacks these entirely, while blistered rock tripe has raised bumps rather than flat granules.

Frosted rock tripe stands out from its rock tripe relatives by its distinctive pale, powdery surface - smooth rock tripe is darker and glossy, while blistered rock tripe has obvious bubble-like bumps.
Among New England's rock tripes, Greater Salted Rocktripe stands out for its large size and distinctive white crusty patches.
